segments.text: Right, can everybody hear me at the back? Good. Let us get started, we have a lot to get through today.
Before we begin the new material, a very quick recap of what we did last time on atomic structure.
So we said the atom has a nucleus containing protons and neutrons, and electrons orbiting around it in shells.
The proton has a relative charge of plus one and a relative mass of one. The neutron is neutral, also relative mass one.
And the electron, relative charge minus one, relative mass roughly one over one thousand eight hundred and forty, so essentially negligible.
We also defined the proton number as the number of protons, and the nucleon number as protons plus neutrons together.
And isotopes, remember, are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but a different number of neutrons.
Good. Now today we build directly on that, because isotopes are exactly why we need the idea of relative atomic mass.
So let us write the definition down carefully. Relative atomic mass, symbol A r, is the weighted average mass of the isotopes of an element.
And crucially it is measured relative to one twelfth of the mass of one atom of carbon twelve. That is the standard we compare everything against.
Notice the word weighted. It is not just an ordinary average. We have to take the abundance of each isotope into account.
Let us do chlorine as the classic example. Chlorine has two isotopes, chlorine thirty five and chlorine thirty seven.
The abundances are approximately seventy five percent chlorine thirty five and twenty five percent chlorine thirty seven.
So the weighted average is thirty five times zero point seven five, plus thirty seven times zero point two five.
That gives us twenty six point two five plus nine point two five, which is thirty five point five. And that is the relative atomic mass of chlorine.
Which is why on the periodic table chlorine says thirty five point five and not a whole number. That confuses a lot of students.
No individual chlorine atom weighs thirty five point five. It is an average across the mixture of isotopes as they occur naturally.
Now, where do we get those abundance figures from? This is where the mass spectrometer comes in.
A mass spectrometer separates the isotopes by their mass to charge ratio and gives us a mass spectrum.
On the mass spectrum, the horizontal axis is mass to charge ratio and the vertical axis is relative abundance.
So each peak corresponds to one isotope, and the height of the peak tells you how abundant that isotope is.
Let us read one together. Here we have a spectrum for magnesium with three peaks at twenty four, twenty five and twenty six.
The relative abundances are seventy nine, ten and eleven percent. So multiply each mass by its abundance and divide by one hundred.
Twenty four times seventy nine, plus twenty five times ten, plus twenty six times eleven, all over one hundred.
That comes to twenty four point three two, which is the relative atomic mass of magnesium. Check it against your data booklet.
One more definition before we finish. Relative isotopic mass is the mass of a single isotope, again relative to carbon twelve.
So relative isotopic mass is for one isotope, relative atomic mass is the weighted average of them all. Do not mix those two up in the exam.
For homework, questions one to six on the sheet, all mass spectrum calculations. See you on Wednesday.
